title: Rice Whisky Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: How whisky can be made from rice, how rice behaves in the cooker and still, where koji fits in and what an Indian distillery should check first.
teaser: India grows more rice than almost any grain. Here is what it takes to turn rice into a spirit that can be called whisky.
standfirst: Rice is a cereal, so it can make whisky. It brings a clean, light spirit and a cooking process quite unlike barley. This guide covers how rice is mashed and distilled and the rules that decide what the result can be called.
sections:
Whisky is a spirit distilled from fermented cereal grain and matured in wood. Rice is a cereal, so in principle it qualifies. In practice, whether a rice spirit can be labelled whisky depends on each market's rules. Some definitions require malt enzymes for converting starch. Others allow other enzymes. India's rules for whisky are set nationally and can change, so check the current notification for your product.

Rice is already a major grain for Indian distilleries. Broken rice is widely used to make grain spirit. A rice whisky asks a different question of the same grain: can it carry character into the cask rather than being distilled out to neutral?
What rice brings and what it lacks

Milled rice is mostly starch, often around 75 to 80% of dry weight, with little protein and almost no fibre. That means high potential yield per tonne. It also means rice has no husk to form a filter bed, no enzymes of its own and very little of the nitrogen yeast needs.

So a rice mash needs an enzyme source and a yeast nutrient plan. The enzymes can come from malted barley, from commercial enzymes or, in East Asian tradition, from koji. Our guide to grains in whisky compares rice with the other cereals.

Rice starch gelatinises at a higher temperature than barley starch, commonly in the range of about 68 to 78 °C depending on the variety. Distillers usually cook milled or broken rice well above that, close to boiling, with a heat stable alpha-amylase to thin the mash. The mash is then cooled before malt or other enzymes go in to finish conversion.

Without a thinning enzyme, a rice cook turns into a thick paste that scorches easily. On a direct fired pot, that paste can burn on within minutes. Steam jackets and agitators are worth having.
Koji, malt and the definition question

Koji is rice or another grain grown with the mould Aspergillus oryzae. It produces enzymes that turn starch into sugar and is central to Japanese sake and shochu. Rice spirits made with koji are well established in East Asia. Whether they can be called whisky depends on the market.

The European definition of whisky, for example, requires the cereal mash to be converted by the diastase of malt, with or without other natural enzymes. A rice spirit converted by koji alone may not qualify there. If you plan to export, design the process around the strictest market on your list.

Rice mashes ferment cleanly because there is little protein and fat. The flip side is low free amino nitrogen, so yeast can stall without added nutrient. Measure gravity twice a day for the first few batches. A fermentation that slows well before reaching its expected final gravity is often short of nitrogen.

Temperature control matters in Indian conditions. Rice washes fermented in the mid 20s °C are usually cleaner than those left to climb past 32 °C, where yeast stress and bacteria both rise.

Rice can give a high yield of alcohol per tonne because so much of the grain is starch. Track your result as litres of pure alcohol per tonne and compare it with the starch content on the supplier's certificate. A gap between the two points to incomplete cooking, poor conversion or a stalled fermentation. A good habit is to run an iodine test on a sample of the mash after conversion: blue black means starch remains.

Rice spirit tends to be light, clean and slightly floral or sweet. Distilled in a pot still and cut with care, it can carry those notes into the cask. Distilled to very high strength in a column, it becomes close to neutral.

Because the spirit is delicate, cask choice shows strongly. A refill or ex-bourbon cask lets the rice character stay visible. A fresh sherry or virgin oak cask can bury it. In Indian heat, delicate spirits can be overwhelmed by oak quickly, so sample often. Our guide to malt, grain and blended whisky places rice whisky among the wider family.

India grows many rice varieties, from fragrant basmati to short grain regional types. For a distillery, broken rice is the usual starting point because it is cheaper than whole grain. Each lot should be checked for moisture, starch content and foreign matter. Some distillers experiment with aromatic or heritage rice for a premium spirit, though whether those aromas survive distillation and maturation is something only trials can show.

Start with a 20 litre pilot mash: cook broken rice with alpha-amylase, cool it, add your chosen malt or enzyme, ferment with a measured nutrient dose and record gravity daily. Distil in a small pot still and nose the hearts diluted to 20% ABV. Those notes, compared against a malt spirit made the same way, will tell you whether rice gives you something worth bottling.
faqs: Can whisky be made from rice?
Rice is a cereal, so it can be used to make whisky. Whether the result can be labelled whisky depends on each market's rules about enzymes and maturation.
No. Shochu is a separate Japanese spirit category, usually converted with koji and often unaged. It is not sold as whisky.
Why do rice mashes need extra yeast nutrient?
Milled rice has very little protein, so the mash is low in the free amino nitrogen yeast needs. Without added nutrient, fermentation can slow or stall.
At what temperature does rice starch gelatinise?
Commonly in the range of about 68 to 78 °C depending on the variety. Distillers usually cook it hotter with a thinning enzyme.
